questions.statement: Which sentence in Andres's paragraph states the main idea?
questions.context: Andres writes a paragraph about the coffee farms he visited in Tarrazu.

options.text: Coffee farming in the Tarrazu valley has changed over the last decade.
options.feedback: Correct: it names the topic and adds the writer's angle, so it can control every other sentence.

options.text: The road up to the farm is steep and the turns are very narrow.
options.feedback: This is a supporting detail about the road, but it cannot carry the whole main idea.

options.text: My uncle grows coffee on three hectares near San Marcos.
options.feedback: It is a personal example about one relative, so it narrows the focus too much.

options.text: Last March I drank four cups of coffee in a single morning.
options.feedback: A funny anecdote that stands alone and does not build any general idea.

questions.explanation:
A topic sentence announces the general idea and usually comes first. Every sentence after it adds reasons, details or examples that stay inside the frame it sets.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence should Karla cut because it breaks paragraph unity?
questions.context: Karla writes about how she prepared for the English exam at her school in Heredia.

options.text: I made a vocabulary list and reviewed it every night for a month.
options.feedback: This is a concrete action that supports the topic and gives evidence for the habit.

options.text: My teacher suggested practice tests from the ministry website.
options.feedback: It names a useful source of practice, so it explains how she actually prepared.

options.text: Last summer my cousin won a prize in mathematics in Limon.
options.feedback: Correct to cut: it changes person, place and subject, so it breaks unity with the topic.

options.text: On exam day I felt nervous, but I answered every single item.
options.feedback: It reports her feelings on exam day, which belongs to the preparation topic.

questions.explanation:
Unity means every sentence in a paragraph develops one single idea. A true detail about an unrelated event is still off topic and weakens the focus, so it is cut or moved.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which topic sentence best suits a paragraph about that market?
questions.context: Steven plans a paragraph that describes the Saturday market in Alajuela.

options.text: The Alajuela Saturday market sells vegetables that taste wonderful.
options.feedback: It limits the paragraph to produce and its quality, so crafts would fall outside the frame.

options.text: The Alajuela Saturday market, a lively tradition, offers produce and crafts.
options.feedback: Correct: it names the place, adds detail, and is broad enough to hold the whole paragraph.

options.text: Last Saturday, after breakfast, we left the house at seven in the morning.
options.feedback: It narrates the speaker's morning, but it never says what the paragraph is about.

options.text: Marta and I carried four bags because the stalls close at noon.
options.feedback: It is only a detail, and without a main idea first the reader has no frame.

questions.explanation:
A good topic sentence names the subject and covers the whole paragraph. It must also be a little broader than any single detail that follows, or those details fall outside its range.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which order is the most logical for Yendry's paragraph about her garden?
questions.context: Yendry explains in one paragraph how she planted a vegetable garden in Heredia.

options.text: Conclusion first, then the topic sentence, then the supporting sentences.
options.feedback: Starting with the conclusion inverts the path, because the idea must be announced first.

options.text: Supporting sentences, then the conclusion, then the topic sentence.
options.feedback: Details before the main idea leave the reader guessing, and nothing has been opened yet.

options.text: Topic sentence, then the conclusion, then the supporting sentences.
options.feedback: The conclusion arrives before the support, so it has nothing to summarise.

options.text: Topic sentence, then the details in time order, then the conclusion.
options.feedback: Correct: the idea is announced, developed step by step, and then closed with a summary.

questions.explanation:
The standard path is topic sentence, then supporting sentences following a clear sequence, then a concluding sentence. Time order or numbered steps belong in the middle of the paragraph.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence links those two study habits with the right logical relation?
questions.context: Alonso compares studying in the cloud forest near Monteverde with studying in town.

options.text: By contrast, the library in town is quiet but it closes early.
options.feedback: Correct: 'By contrast' marks a difference, which is exactly the link between the two situations.

options.text: As a result, Alonso now studies in the forest when the weather is fine.
options.feedback: 'As a result' signals a consequence, yet the two habits are alternatives and not effects.

options.text: For example, he carries a notebook and two pens to the reserve.
options.feedback: 'For example' introduces evidence, so a general claim has to come before it.

options.text: In the same way, both places suit students who read a lot.
options.feedback: 'In the same way' joins similar points, but these two places are opposed and not parallel.

questions.explanation:
Connectives must match the real logical link. Contrast words signal difference, cause words signal a result, and example words signal support, so a wrong link misleads the reader.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence correctly links the dry week to the park's decision?
questions.context: It did not rain for a week in Braulio Carrillo, and the park made a decision.

options.text: However, the park reopened the trail so hikers could walk again.
options.feedback: 'However' signals contrast, but no opposing idea appears here, only a cause and its effect.

options.text: As a result, the park reopened the trail so hikers could walk again.
options.feedback: Correct: 'As a result' presents the dry week as the cause and the reopening as the effect.

options.text: In addition, the park reopened the trail so hikers could walk again.
options.feedback: 'In addition' adds extra weight, yet the second sentence is a consequence and not a bonus point.

options.text: Otherwise, the park reopened the trail so hikers could walk again.
options.feedback: 'Otherwise' shows what happens if a condition fails, which is hypothetical here.

questions.explanation:
Cause and effect paragraphs place the cause before the effect and use a signal word such as 'as a result' or 'because'. The connective must confirm that real relationship.

---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which closing sentence best suits Paola's paragraph on planting trees?
questions.context: Paola writes a persuasive paragraph arguing that her town should plant more trees.

options.text: On the first Saturday of the month, forty neighbours came with spades.
options.feedback: A concrete example that supports the argument, but it is not a closing move.

options.text: The city has three parks and one very small playground for children.
options.feedback: A neutral fact about facilities that ends the paragraph without any conclusion.

options.text: Trees give shade, absorb carbon dioxide and reduce noise on busy roads.
options.feedback: This is a body sentence with reasons, so it belongs before the closing appeal.

options.text: If the council approves the plan, our streets will be cooler next summer.
options.feedback: Correct: a persuasive paragraph usually closes with a recommendation tied to its topic.

questions.explanation:
A concluding sentence may summarise the main point or, in persuasive writing, recommend an action. It should never open a new idea that the paragraph never developed.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version of Julio's paragraph avoids unnecessary repetition?
questions.context: Julio wrote a short paragraph about the bike ride from his house to school in San Jose.

options.text: I cycle to school every morning, and the ride takes about twenty minutes.
options.feedback: Correct: one idea, one clean pair of clauses, and no fact is stated twice.

options.text: I cycle to school every single morning, and in the morning I cycle to school.
options.feedback: 'Every morning' and 'in the morning' repeat the same time, so one of them should go.

options.text: Cycling is something I do, and my activity in the morning is cycling too.
options.feedback: This is wordy nominalisation, because the action is hidden inside nouns instead of verbs.

options.text: I cycle, I also pedal, and furthermore I ride my bicycle to school.
options.feedback: Three verbs describe one single action, so the paragraph swells without gaining meaning.

questions.explanation:
A tight paragraph states each point once. Repeating a time phrase, hiding the action inside nouns, or stacking synonyms all add length without adding information for the reader.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which detail best supports Milena's claim about job options?
questions.context: Milena's paragraph claims that learning English opens better job options in Heredia.

options.text: Her English teacher always wears a red scarf on Friday mornings.
options.feedback: A detail about clothing that neither shows an employer nor proves anything about jobs.

options.text: English is spoken in many countries around the world today.
options.feedback: It is a true general fact, but it names no local outcome, so it stays outside her claim.

options.text: Her cousin got a tourism job in Heredia after passing an English exam.
options.feedback: Correct: it shows a real job in Heredia that followed from English, so it proves her point.

options.text: English has a very large number of words and irregular verbs.
options.feedback: This describes the language itself, not the effect English had on anyone's employment.

questions.explanation:
Supporting sentences must be relevant and concrete. Strong support names the same actors and the same outcome as the topic sentence, so the reader can accept the general claim.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the main structural fault in the last sentence of his paragraph?
questions.context: Ramon wrote a paragraph about recycling and closed it with a soccer tournament.

options.text: It repeats the topic sentence word for word at the end.
options.feedback: Repetition is not the problem here, because the fault is the new content the paragraph never set up.

options.text: It introduces new information that the paragraph never developed.
options.feedback: Correct: a concluding sentence must wrap up the developed idea and never open a fresh topic.

options.text: It is too short to be accepted as a real sentence.
options.feedback: A short sentence can summarise perfectly well, so length is not a test of a conclusion.

options.text: It contains a spelling mistake in its second word.
options.feedback: That is a mechanics matter, and the sentence here is spelled correctly and structurally complete.

questions.explanation:
A concluding sentence may summarise, restate a general point or recommend an action, but it must stay inside the paragraph's topic. New facts belong in a new paragraph.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence opens an argumentative paragraph rather than a descriptive one?
questions.context: Teacher Silvia asks her grade 11 class to write four different kinds of paragraph.

options.text: At six the coffee farm wakes up, and the pickers arrive before the sun.
options.feedback: This is a narrative opening with a time sequence, so it tells an event instead of arguing.

options.text: The beans dry on patios for up to twelve days under a thin cloth.
options.feedback: This describes a process step by step, so it informs the reader about what happens.

options.text: Small coffee growers deserve higher prices than the market now offers.
options.feedback: Correct: it states a debatable claim that evidence in the paragraph could defend.

options.text: Green hills roll north from Turrialba toward the Caribbean lowlands.
options.feedback: A descriptive sentence about the landscape, which paints a picture and takes no stand.

questions.explanation:
An argumentative paragraph opens with a claim and then defends it with evidence. Descriptive and narrative paragraphs give pictures or events, so they never ask the reader to accept a position.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sequence keeps his process paragraph logically clear?
questions.context: Luis writes a process paragraph explaining how he brews coffee at home.

options.text: Grind the beans, heat the water, filter the grounds, then pour the coffee.
options.feedback: Correct: every step grows out of the previous one, so the reader can follow the method.

options.text: Drink the coffee, grind the beans, heat the water, filter the grounds.
options.feedback: Drinking comes first here, which reverses the process before anything has been made.

options.text: Heat the water, drink the coffee, pour the coffee, grind the beans.
options.feedback: Drinking and pouring appear before heating and grinding, so the order breaks in the middle.

options.text: Grind the beans, filter the grounds, drink the coffee, heat the water.
options.feedback: Filtering and drinking arrive before heating and pouring, so the sequence collapses early.

questions.explanation:
In a process paragraph the middle part follows a natural order, usually time. Signal words such as 'then' and 'after that' make that order visible to the reader.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence is the strongest thesis for Esteban's paragraph on transport?
questions.context: Esteban must state a clear thesis for a paragraph about public transport in San Jose.

options.text: Buses in San Jose are sometimes late, and the roads are busy at seven.
options.feedback: It offers two observations only, and a thesis must take a position that evidence can support.

options.text: Public transport is a topic that everybody in the capital can discuss.
options.feedback: It announces a topic but takes no stand, so there is nothing there for the paragraph to argue.

options.text: There are many buses, and there are also trams, and there are routes.
options.feedback: It merely counts the services and repeats the same opening, so no argument appears.

options.text: Because buses are slow and overcrowded, the city should invest in rail.
options.feedback: Correct: it states what the city should do and gives the reason the evidence will confirm.

questions.explanation:
A strong thesis combines a claim about what should happen with the reason behind it. That reason tells the reader which evidence belongs in the paragraph and which does not.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which description shows a correctly organised paragraph?
questions.context: Reviewers must choose the best structured paragraph among three student submissions.

options.text: A topic sentence at the end, two details, and then no conclusion at all.
options.feedback: With the main idea at the end, the reader must guess the focus while reading the details.

options.text: A topic sentence, three linked details, and a closing summary of the point.
options.feedback: Correct: the idea is announced, the details develop it in order, and the last sentence closes it.

options.text: Four unrelated facts and no topic sentence anywhere in the paragraph.
options.feedback: Without a topic sentence the paragraph has no focus, and separate facts cannot hold together.

options.text: A topic sentence, one very long sentence, and then the paragraph stops.
options.feedback: One sentence cannot develop an idea, and no closing sentence means the paragraph stops abruptly.

questions.explanation:
A well built paragraph follows a predictable path: main idea, development, closing. Clear structural marks let the reader follow the argument without guessing what each part is for.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which item should Nadia move to a separate paragraph?
questions.context: Nadia notices that her essay places two different main ideas in a single paragraph.

options.text: Her first idea, which already has three supporting sentences.
options.feedback: That idea is already supported, so nothing in its structure requires a new paragraph.

options.text: The example about her grandfather's farm in Bagaces.
options.feedback: An example belongs inside the paragraph it illustrates, and moving it breaks that link.

options.text: A second idea about noise levels in her neighbourhood.
options.feedback: Correct: two main ideas in one paragraph destroy unity, since a paragraph develops only one.

options.text: The closing sentence that summarises her first idea.
options.feedback: A closing sentence stays at the end of the paragraph whose idea it summarises.

questions.explanation:
When one paragraph carries two main ideas, neither is developed well. Split where the writer changes subject, then give each new paragraph its own topic sentence and support.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which revision would best improve the structure of Carlos's paragraph?
questions.context: Carlos wrote a paragraph about saving water that begins in the middle of the idea.

options.text: Add two more sentences so the paragraph becomes longer and richer.
options.feedback: More length never fixes a missing opening, because the reader still cannot see the focus.

options.text: Copy the whole paragraph onto a new page and begin again there.
options.feedback: Changing the page changes nothing, since what matters is the order of the ideas inside.

options.text: Repeat the first sentence at the end to close the paragraph.
options.feedback: Copying a sentence creates redundancy, and a real conclusion has to develop the point.

options.text: Add a topic sentence at the start and group the details under it.
options.feedback: Correct: a clear topic sentence sets the focus and grouping the details restores unity.

questions.explanation:
Editing a paragraph means checking its structure, not only its grammar: it needs a main idea, an ordered development and a closing sentence, each in its proper place.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence avoids repetition while keeping a clear reference?
questions.context: Maria's paragraph names the new aqueduct in Alajuela and must keep the link clear.

options.text: Nevertheless, the new aqueduct was opened in Alajuela last year.
options.feedback: 'Nevertheless' signals contrast, yet no previous sentence states an opposing idea.

options.text: Opened in Alajuela last year, the structure is still in use today.
options.feedback: Correct: an alternative name keeps the reference clear without repeating the same noun.

options.text: It is very long, and it is also expensive, and it is also modern.
options.feedback: Stacking 'it is' clauses with 'also' adds no information and blurs the reference.

options.text: Alajuela, a city in the valley, is a city that has an aqueduct.
options.feedback: This shifts the focus to the city, so the paragraph describes a place and not the aqueduct.

questions.explanation:
Coherence depends on clear references. Repeating the exact noun is safe, but a careless chain of empty pronouns forces the reader to guess which noun the pronoun stands for.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which version shows elaboration instead of a bare list of facts?
questions.context: Elena's paragraph about the Monteverde cloud forest lists facts but explains nothing.

options.text: The cloud forest is wet, it is green, it is cool and it is quiet.
options.feedback: Four simple predicates pile up facts, yet no sentence explains why any of them matters.

options.text: Many birds live there, and there are also frogs and also butterflies.
options.feedback: Every sentence repeats the same pattern and 'also' adds nothing to the information.

options.text: Quetzal birds live in the cloud forest, and the cool damp air suits them.
options.feedback: Correct: the sentence links a fact about the bird to a reason, which is real elaboration.

options.text: Monteverde has a cloud forest, and Costa Rica has many green forests.
options.feedback: It repeats two similar facts and develops neither, so the reader gains almost nothing.

questions.explanation:
Elaboration means adding an explanation, a reason or an example after a fact. A paragraph of unlinked statements stays flat because each point is left undeveloped.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which closing sentence suits Hector's narrative paragraph about the storm?
questions.context: Hector writes a narrative paragraph about a storm that hit the coast near Nicoya.

options.text: Finally the wind stopped, and the family saw no damage to the roof.
options.feedback: Correct: it narrates the last action and closes the story by showing the danger passed.

options.text: Storms near Nicoya usually arrive between May and November every year.
options.feedback: A general fact opens a new idea here, and the story never set that up.

options.text: The best hurricane plan for any family includes three steps and supplies.
options.feedback: It jumps to advice the paragraph never gave, so it belongs in a different text.

options.text: In conclusion, the text above has described a storm in the south.
options.feedback: A comment on the text itself tells the reader nothing about the outcome of the event.

questions.explanation:
Narrative paragraphs usually end with the last event of the story. A closing sentence that generalises or comments on the text breaks the time frame the reader has been following.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which plan best improves Rosa's repetitive draft paragraph?
questions.context: Rosa reviews a draft paragraph in which the same idea appears four times.

options.text: Add more examples of the same point to make the paragraph look richer.
options.feedback: More examples of a point already made four times adds length and repetition together.

options.text: Change the font and the spacing so the repetition becomes less visible.
options.feedback: Presentation changes how a paragraph looks, but not the fact that the idea repeats.

options.text: Split the paragraph into four shorter paragraphs, one for each repetition.
options.feedback: Repeating the same point in four paragraphs multiplies the problem instead of solving it.

options.text: Merge the repeated points, keep the best example, then state the conclusion.
options.feedback: Correct: merging removes the redundancy, and one example plus a closing sentence gives unity.

questions.explanation:
Revision works on structure before surface form: merge repeated ideas, keep only the strongest evidence, and finish with a sentence that closes the single focus of the paragraph.
